findings.title: Cisco Expressway Series Remote Code Execution Vulnerability
findings.summary: A vulnerability in the database service feature of Cisco Expressway Series could allow an unauthenticated, remote attacker with network access to a Cisco Expressway device to execute arbitrary operating system commands as root . This vulnerability is due to the use of persistent cookies. Additionally, there is insufficient validation of client certificates when the TLS Verify Mode is set to Enabled for clustering, which means that client certificates are not validated. An attacker with possession of the cookies could exploit this vulnerability by connecting to the database service and invoking specific remote procedure call (RPC) commands. A successful exploit could allow the attacker to execute arbitrary commands as root on the underlying operating system of an affected device. Note: Cisco Expressway Series refers to Cisco Expressway Core (Expressway-C) devices and Cisco Expressway Edge (Expressway-E) devices. Cisco has released software updates that address this vulnerability. There are no workarounds that address this vulnerability. This advisory is available at the following link: https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-vcs-static-cred-hr7EWZ8t This advisory is part of a group of advisories. For a complete list of the advisories and links to them, see Cisco Advance Notification for Publication of October 21, 2026, Security Advisories . In addition, for further documentation of improvements and fixes in Cisco Expressway Series see Cisco Expressway Series Security Hardening Release: October 2026 . Security Impact Rating: Critical CVE: CVE-2026-76466

secp256k1-native has a compiler-induced timing side channel in scalar multiplication
findings.summary:
## Summary

`Point#mul` — the default, constant-time scalar multiplication and the library's headline secret-scalar operation — could leak timing information about the secret scalar (a private key or ECDSA-style nonce in a downstream consumer) **not because of a source-level bug, but because the compiler reconstructed a branch from branchless source.**

The Montgomery ladder selects between point candidates with `uint256_select`, written deliberately branchlessly as `r = (a & ~mask) | (b & mask)` with a mask that is all-ones or all-zeros. GCC 15.2 at `-O2` recognises this select idiom, reconstructs the original boolean condition, and emits a secret-dependent conditional jump (`je`/`jne`). The branch's taken/not-taken timing correlates with the secret scalar bits flowing through the ladder.

This silently undid the 0.17.0 fix for the historical |t|=875 infinity-branch leak, which had relied on `uint256_select` compiling to branchless code.

## Impact

A timing side-channel on the secret scalar in constant-time scalar multiplication. For a consumer that calls `Point#mul` (or the native `scalar_multiply_ct`) on a secret key or nonce and exposes timing to an attacker (e.g. an online signing oracle), repeated measurements can statistically recover scalar bits — the classic ECC private-key/nonce timing-attack setting (cf. Brumley–Boneh). The leak is in the *compiled binary*; the source is correct, so source review and the deterministic ctgrind check on a *non-reconstructing* toolchain do not reveal it.

Pre-1.0 with no published RubyGems dependents, so this is handled as fix-publish-and-document: full GHSA + CVE record without a coordinated downstream-notification timeline. The CVE is filed for citability so the empirical record (paper → review → compiler regression → fix) is permanent and searchable.

findings.title: Vulnerability in Oracle OpenJDK (Java4Shell) Affecting Cisco Products: November 2026
findings.summary: On November 17, 2026, Oracle announced the availability of fixes for a vulnerability in OpenJDK that could lead to remote code execution identified by CVE-2026-114938. The vulnerability affects OpenJDK Java 17.0.6 and later on x86-64 platforms when processing Base64 encoded content. For more information, see the Oracle Critical Security Patch Update Advisory - November 2026 and the OpenJDK Vulnerability Advisory: 2026/11/17 . For additional information, see the Talos blog post: Talos Threat Advisory CVE-2026-114938: Critical vulnerability in OpenJDK JAVA This advisory will be updated as additional information becomes available. This advisory is available at the following link: https://sec.cloudapps.cisco.com/security/center/content/CiscoSecurityAdvisory/cisco-sa-nov2026-java-rce-eCa6ss9z Security Impact Rating: High CVE: CVE-2026-114938

findings.title: VirtualBox Process Hardening on Windows 2026 Edition: What’s a Single Bit Between Friends?
findings.summary: Back in 2017 I did some research into Oracle VirtualBox on Windows. Specifically I focussed on their mechanism to protect their VM processes from the user on the host. The protection was to gate who could open the kernel driver, which might allow for privilege escalation due to the way it was designed. At the time I found 3 ways of bypassing the protection, with an additional issue in COM’s runtime I reported in 2020. These issues were all written up in this post . Fast forward to 2026 and I decided to look at VirtualBox again to see if much had changed. This time I found 3 new bypasses for protected processes, with an additional bug which was a broken fix for the 2020 bypass breaking due to changes in Windows. In this blog post I want to focus on one specific issue CVE-2026-87268 which abused a feature of the .NET Framework which, when combined with the implementation of the DLL loader hooks implemented by VirtualBox, permitted a bypass of the checks and allowed me to load arbitrary code into the protected process. Let’s dig into the root cause of the issue in .NET first, before moving on to exploitation in VirtualBox. .NET Assembly Loading The .NET Framework is interesting when it comes to bypassing process hardening as it supports loading assemblies from a memory buffer as long as you stick to only using managed code. This is obviously useful if the hardened process is maintained through verifying what DLLs can or cannot be loaded as it bypasses the traditional image mapping process. As the .NET runtime implementation is Microsoft signed, it’s usually permitted to load by any such checks. The canonical way to load from a memory buffer is to use the Assembly::Load static method which accepts a byte array. This does require you to run some .NET code first, or find a confused deputy to do the work for you.
